credit.credit-words: Modes
A bit of theory
BH
Modes are just alternative arrangements of a scale, starting on a different note.
Modes divide in to two broad groups, the natural modes which are based on the major scale, and artificial modes
where basically anything goes. This discussion only covers the natural modes.
The natural modes can be thought about as "all the white notes starting on X" where X is the note of your choice.
You can of course then transpose that mode into any key signature, but one particularily useful transposition is to
make C the root of the mode. For example the Dorian mode:
can be transposed down a major 2nd to give:
I personally find this second representation, always starting from C, to be easier to think about. You can
immediately see the difference between the mode and the major scale. In this case, Dorian has a minor 7th
and a minor 3rd, but it's not a true minor scale because it has a major sixth.
Another thing to be aware of when looking at a mode is the location of the semitones. To continue our example,
Dorian has a semitone between the second and third scale degree, and between the sixth and seventh scale degree.
Yet another aspect of a mode is the nature of its harmony. We can use roman numerals to describe each triad,
using upper case numerals for major triads and lower case for minor, and indicating the diminished triad with
a suffix
Order of the Natural Modes
Using the second representation of modes, always rooted on the same note (C) we can arrange the modes in order
of the number of sharps or flats. As we remove sharps and add flats, the mood of the mode becomes darker. This
is one of the most musically useful aspects of the modes, They present a continuum of scales from "brighter than
major" to "darker than minor", and each mode has it's own characteristic sound.
In the following, I'll present each of the natural modes in turn, from brightest to darkest, and give either an
existing musical example where possible or a little demonstration of each to help you to remember their sound.
In each of the examples the characteristic notes of the mode are circled to help you identify them.
This is the brightest of the modes, a kind of "extra major" mode. I found it quite difficult to find a good example
in the classical repetoire, the most famous being Beethoven's "Heileger Dankgesang" from his 15th string quartet,
but that's quite long and I don't think it is particularly representative so I've just written a short example.
Because this mode lacks the leading tone (the semitone below the tonic) it has a somewhat melancholy sound,
while the major 3rd categorises it as still being a "major" mode.
The Beatles "Norwegian Wood" is a Mixolydian tune (flat 7th).
This is a very common mode in English folk music and examples abound. Here's a particularily striking one.
Another mode with a ton of examples in folk and pop music. It's almost a minor scale but the major 6th gives
it a slightly less minor feel. Here's a very famous example.
While this is equivalent to the natural minor scale, the natural minor is not really used much in classical music
because it has no leading tone. Normally the 6th and 7th would be raised in ascending melodic minor to give a
better resolution to the tonic, so leaving those notes flattened is characteristic of this mode.
Again examples abound, This one everybody should know.
A "super minor" mode, the characteristic flattened 2nd gives this mode a very stern feel. It is less common than
most of the other modes but there is one very famous example, Thomas Tallis' "Third Tune", the theme of
Vaughan Williams' "Fantasy on a theme by Thomas Tallis". Unlike the other examples this tune does not stay
strictly in the mode, but makes use of a "Picardy third" (major tonic triad) to great effect.
This last mode, because it has a diminished tonic chord, was considered unusable in the past. There are very few
examples that are anything more than experimental, but one noteable exception is the song "Dust to Dust" from
John Kirkpartick. It's very bleak, in keeping with the mode, and is sung unaccompanied.
